title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: We buy the important components from the technology providers and integrate them with our own designs, storage, networking and software. The finished system sells to the customer — we do not rent out GPU capacity.
epigraph.author: Synthesis of Netweb's OEM operating model, FY2026 Annual Report and Q2 FY2027 Earnings Call

web_blocks.html: Netweb's go-to-market model is a hybrid of direct enterprise selling, government and public-sector tendering, and channel-led distribution. All of it wraps around OEM partnerships with the silicon vendors. The company maintains manufacturing and R&D facilities in Delhi-NCR (Faridabad and Gurugram) and Hyderabad, with eighteen offices across India and an office in Singapore. Large sovereign and institutional orders are typically won directly through tenders or negotiated strategic contracts. Enterprise orders arrive both directly and through distributor and system-integrator partners. For example, Netweb's 2026 sovereign cyber-secure compute facility for CERT-IN was disclosed as processed through the company's distributor. Because the customer base is dominated by government, defence, research, banking and large enterprise buyers, the sales cycle is long, qualification-heavy and reference-driven.

The supply chain is the crux of the model and the crux of the risk. Netweb is an OEM, not a chipmaker. It buys GPUs from NVIDIA, CPUs from Intel and AMD, memory from Samsung, and power and cooling components from partners such as Vertiv, then integrates them with its own chassis, board designs and software. CRISIL Ratings (June 2026) quantifies the resulting procurement concentration: Netweb's top three suppliers account for 65–70% of total procurement, with a significant share of critical components imported from Taiwan. In addition, management disclosed on the Q3 FY2026 call that forward contracts cover roughly 60% of import payables, leaving around 40% exposed to USD/INR depreciation between order booking and settlement. Gross margin is set by the spread between component cost and system price, while working capital is set by how long Netweb must hold expensive silicon before delivery. Management is deliberately carrying more inventory — inventory days stood at 117 at September 2026 versus 86 at March 2026 — to secure critical components against long lead times and safeguard execution of a ₹2,629 crore order book. The flip side is equally explicit: if component prices fall, Taiwan shipments disrupt, or customers defer, that inventory loses value.

Pricing varies by segment. AI systems are priced per node or per rack with a service wrapper. Management has said the gross-margin profile of a very large deal is structurally different from a small one. Quarterly gross margin is therefore a function of deal mix and should not be read sequentially. HPC supercomputing projects are priced on a fixed-scope project basis plus a multi-year maintenance contract. Private cloud and HCI carry a hardware-plus-software-subscription-plus-support structure, the closest thing in the portfolio to recurring revenue. Standard execution runs 10 to 16 weeks per order. Billing on large institutional orders is milestone-and-advance based. That is why receivables improved to 62 days in Q2 FY2027 while inventory ballooned. Customers pay promptly once a milestone is met, but Netweb has already funded the components.

web_blocks.caption: Table 3.1: Netweb Technologies Audited FY2026 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Scaled to ₹100 Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: For every ₹100 of FY2026 audited revenue, ₹79.15 went into materials and inventory build, ₹7.81 covered employee (-₹3.68) and operating overhead (-₹4.13), and ₹13.04 became operating EBITDA. After interest, tax, and working-capital shifts, ₹7.83 arrived as operating cash flow and ₹7.37 as free cash flow after -₹0.46 of capex. The gap between ₹9.43 of accounting profit and ₹7.37 of free cash flow captures the integrator model: profit is earned on the income statement, then collected only when inventory converts.

web_blocks.html: The cash-conversion mechanics deserve particular care, because they carry a real financing drag that does not show up in headline EBITDA. Receivable days were 112 in FY2026 on Screener's annualised basis and improved to 62 in Q2 FY2027, while inventory days rose to 117 and the cash-conversion cycle stretched to 94 days against 84 days for FY2026 (within management's 90–110 day guidance). Funding that cycle required a rapid expansion of both equity and bank lines: of the ₹1,200 crore QIP raised on 20 August 2026, roughly ₹766.7 crore (~64%) was already absorbed into working capital within forty days by 30 September 2026 (leaving ~₹425.6 crore unutilised), while CRISIL expanded rated bank facilities 3.46x from ₹700 crore to ₹2,420 crore in June 2026 (₹2,150 crore fund-based working-capital lines plus ₹270 crore non-fund/bank-guarantee limits). Even though quarter-end net cash stood at ₹13.6 crore, intra-quarter working-capital borrowings and LC/BG fees drove quarterly finance costs up 26x YoY from ₹0.9 crore in Q2 FY2026 to ₹23.8 crore in Q2 FY2027 (₹46 crore TTM) — a material hidden friction on unit economics.

web_blocks.title: Unit Economics: What a ₹100 AI Order Actually Earns
paragraphs: Strip the project accounting away and Netweb's economics per order are those of an advanced integrator. A large AI system carries roughly 13–15% operating EBITDA margin — so on a ₹100 system, the company keeps around ₹13–14 of operating profit. From that it funds engineering, R&D, sales, interest on the working-capital borrowing used to buy the components, and tax, leaving roughly ₹8–9 of bottom-line profit if collections are timely.

The critical variable is not the margin percentage; it is the time between paying the component supplier and being paid by the customer. If that gap is 90–110 days, the company must finance a full system's worth of components from its own balance sheet and its borrowings for a quarter. That is why a ₹1,200 crore equity raise was necessary even while the company reported record profits: growth, not profitability, is what consumes the cash. The unit economics work as long as order intake keeps growing and customers keep paying on schedule; they reverse sharply if either stops.

web_blocks.html: Two structural features of the distribution model remain genuine positives, though both carry real limits uncovered in our forensic review. First, Netweb holds chip-agnostic OEM partnerships across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel and can re-schematic designs over a two-to-three-year roadmap. In practice, however, CRISIL (June 2026) notes that the top three suppliers still account for 65–70% of procurement, so near-term supply concentration remains high. Second, PLI 1.0 and 2.0 qualification supports domestic-content eligibility on sovereign and defence tenders. Yet India's PLI 2.0 IT Hardware scheme approved 27 beneficiaries — including Dell, HP, Foxconn, Lenovo/Dixon, VVDN, and Kaynes — which narrows that domestic-manufacturing edge in commercial AI servers.

book_paragraphs: Let us follow one rupee of Netweb revenue from the customer's purchase order all the way to free cash flow, because the journey tells you more about this company than any margin ratio. The order arrives, usually after a long qualification — a government tender, a defence procurement, a bank's technology committee, or a hyperscaler's engineering review. Netweb wins the contract on integration capability, made-in-India eligibility and price. Then comes the part that shapes the whole business: before it can deliver anything, it must buy the GPUs, the memory, the CPUs and the cooling from its partners, and it must pay for them long before the customer pays Netweb.

Picture the supply chain as a physical chain with Netweb in the middle. On one side sit the technology vendors — NVIDIA for accelerators, Intel and AMD for CPUs, Samsung for memory, Vertiv for power and cooling. CRISIL's June 2026 credit review puts a stark number on that dependence: Netweb's top three suppliers account for 65–70% of procurement, with a heavy share of components imported from Taiwan, and management hedges only about 60% of its import payables via forward contracts. Netweb buys those components and adds its own chassis design, board design, storage, networking and software. On the other side sits the customer, who wants a working system, not a pile of parts. Netweb's gross margin is simply the spread between what the components cost and what the integrated system fetches; its cash flow is simply how long it must hold those components before the customer's payment arrives.

Now read Table 3.1, the ₹100 waterfall, and notice how much of each hundred rupees is consumed before anything is earned. Exactly ₹79.15 goes to materials and inventory build, and ₹7.81 covers employee costs (-₹3.68) and operating overhead (-₹4.13), leaving ₹13.04 of operating EBITDA. After interest — the company was carrying ₹333 crore of borrowings at September 2026, largely to fund that inventory — after tax and depreciation, and after working-capital shifts, ₹7.83 arrives as operating cash flow and ₹7.37 survives as free cash flow after ₹0.46 of capex. That is a healthy number, and it is also a fragile one, because it depends on the time gap between paying suppliers and being paid.

This is why you should watch both the cash-conversion cycle and the finance-cost line as closely as EBITDA. At September 2026 the cycle reached 94 days, with receivables an impressive 62 days but inventory a heavy 117 days. Ask yourself why a company that just raised ₹1,200 crore in August 2026 and reported ₹13.6 crore of net cash still saw quarterly finance costs surge 26-fold year on year to ₹23.8 crore in Q2 FY2027 (₹46 crore trailing twelve months). The answer is working-capital intensity: ₹766.7 crore of the QIP — nearly two-thirds — was absorbed into working capital within forty days, while CRISIL expanded rated bank facilities from ₹700 crore to ₹2,420 crore to back intra-quarter GPU import financing and ₹270 crore of non-fund bank guarantees. Management calls the inventory build deliberate; a sceptic would call it an expensive bet. Both descriptions are true, and the difference only becomes visible if demand slows.

Distribution here is not the glamorous kind. There is no consumer brand and no viral product. Instead there is a factory in Faridabad, eighteen offices across India, an office in Singapore, a distributor channel for some orders, and a set of OEM partnerships that took years to earn. The distribution edge is domestic qualification and sovereign-HPC provenance: on defence and research tenders mandating Indian design and local assembly, Netweb competes against a narrow field. In commercial AI servers, however, India's PLI 2.0 IT Hardware scheme has approved 27 beneficiaries — including Dell, HP, Foxconn, Lenovo via Dixon, VVDN, and Kaynes — meaning local manufacturing alone is no longer an exclusive shield.

The chip-agnostic partnership structure is a helpful design option, though not immunity from vendor concentration. Because Netweb builds on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel platforms, management can re-schematic designs over a two-to-three-year roadmap as architectures evolve. Yet CRISIL's disclosure that the top three suppliers still drive 65–70% of procurement is a stark reminder that Netweb's core silicon remains its partners' technology — its own contribution is integration, manufacturing and support, which are competitive strengths rather than monopolies.

So when you size this business, hold two truths together. The unit economics are genuinely attractive for an integrator: ₹13–14 of operating profit on every ₹100 sold, improving with scale. And the cash economics are genuinely demanding: growth, not profit, is what eats the balance sheet. Every rupee of revenue growth pulls more cash into inventory before it returns as cash from operations. That is exactly why the ₹1,200 crore raise happened in the same quarter as record profits, and it is the pattern you must keep watching in every future quarter.

Let me make the cash lesson concrete with a simple question you can ask of any fast-growing hardware company. If the company stopped growing tomorrow, would it generate a lot of cash or a little? For Netweb the honest answer is a lot, because a freeze on new orders would let the inventory liquidate, receivables convert and borrowings unwind. That is a comforting answer, and it is also the trap. A business that only generates cash when it stops growing is a business whose growth you must finance, and whose stall you must survive. Netweb is not fragile — it earns good margins, its customers are creditworthy and its balance sheet is now well funded. But it is a business that rewards a shareholder who understands the financing as clearly as the engineering. That understanding is exactly what this chapter is for.

book_callouts.title: Why Growth Consumes Cash Here
book_callouts.text: In a software business, growth produces cash because an extra customer costs almost nothing to serve. In Netweb's business, growth consumes cash because every extra rupee of revenue must first be spent on components. A company growing revenue 90% a year can be profitable and still need fresh capital, and that is not a red flag by itself — it is the arithmetic of a physical integrator. The red flag would be if the growth stopped while the inventory stayed on the books.
